nameStory: St. Lucie cherry gets its name from the French port city of Saint-Lucie, though it's also called mahaleb cherry after its scientific name. This European native has been cultivated for centuries not for its fruit, but for the fragrant seeds inside its cherry pits, which are ground into a prized spice used in Middle Eastern and European baking.
description: St. Lucie cherry is a small to medium-sized tree that rarely grows taller than 20-25 feet in New England. This European import has an open, somewhat irregular crown with spreading branches. It produces clusters of small white flowers in spring, followed by tiny black cherries that are barely a third of an inch across. The tree is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers bloom in loose, drooping clusters of 6-10 blossoms in late spring, each with five rounded petals and a sweet, almond-like fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny black cherries, smaller than a pea, ripen in summer; the seeds inside have a distinctive sweet-bitter almond scent when crushed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are 1-3 inches long with finely toothed edges, dark green above and paler below, arranged alternately along branches

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish bark becomes slightly furrowed with age, often developing a reddish-brown tint on younger branches

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree or large shrub with an open, irregular crown and somewhat drooping branches that create a graceful, fountain-like appearance

habitat: In its native range, St. Lucie cherry grows on rocky slopes and dry, limestone soils. In New England, it would most likely be found as an escaped ornamental or remnant planting near old homesteads or abandoned gardens. It prefers well-drained, alkaline soils and full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters appear in May, filling the air with a sweet, almond-like fragrance that's strongest on warm afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Small black cherries ripen by midsummer, and the tree's distinctive scented seeds can be detected by crushing the pits.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange before dropping, and the tree's irregular branching pattern becomes more visible.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the tree's open, fountain-like growth habit, with smooth gray bark and small, pointed buds.

funFact: The seeds of St. Lucie cherry are ground into a spice called 'mahlab' that's essential in Greek Easter bread and Middle Eastern pastries - bakers prize these tiny seeds so highly that they're sometimes called 'cherry vanilla' and can cost more per pound than vanilla beans!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with chokecherry, but St. Lucie cherry has much smaller fruit (pea-sized vs. grape-sized) and distinctive almond-scented seeds. Remember: if the crushed pit smells like marzipan, you've found St. Lucie cherry.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a cherry, St. Lucie cherry is grown primarily as a rootstock for grafting other stone fruits rather than for its own fruit. The tree's rarity in New England means most encounters would likely be near old farm sites or botanical collections.
compareHints: St. Lucie cherry stands out from other New England cherries by its exceptionally small fruit size and the distinctive almond fragrance of its crushed seeds. Unlike our native black cherry with its long flower clusters, or chokecherry with its larger berries, St. Lucie cherry produces tiny fruits in loose, drooping clusters. The sweet-bitter almond scent when you crack open the pit is unique among our regional Prunus species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
